newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Suspected Loyalist bomb found near Irish border.
newsitem.headline: Suspected Loyalist bomb found near Irish border.

text.p: Irish army experts on Sunday carried out a controlled explosion on a suspected bomb which was thought planted by Northern Ireland Protestant extremists in the border town of Dundalk.
Police said they received a coded warning about a package left in an alley in the main street of Dundalk, about five miles (eight km) from the border with British-ruled Northern Ireland.
A telephone caller to a Belfast newspaper said he represented a "Loyalist Paramilitary Organisation" but did not say which of Northern Ireland's Loyalist organisations he represented.
The caller said a device had also been planted at Dublin airport but nothing was found.
Loyalists are supposed to be observing a truce since October 1994 as part of Northern Ireland's slow-moving peace process.
They have waged a guerrilla campaign against Irish and Catholic targets to keep Northern Ireland British and want the Irish government to drop a constitutional claim to the province.
The device was planted days before Ireland's June 6 election in a major town on the main Belfast to Dublin road.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA), which is fighting a rival guerrilla war to end British rule, disrupted traffic and daily life during Britain's April election campaign with a series of bomb warnings, both hoax and real.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on hearing of the controlled explosion: "Obviously this reminds us of the need to maintain a very vigilant security presence with regard to paramilitary activity."
Police said the device appeared similar to one used in an attack on the offices of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing in March. Its detonator went off, but not the explosive.
They said a detonator, alarm clock and what was thought to be a commercial explosive appeared to have been packed into a thermos flask. The detonator exploded harmlessly, they said.
Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, are officially observing a truce which they called in October 1994 to match a now-broken IRA truce.
But a spate of recent attacks has been blamed by Northern Ireland police on a variety of Loyalist groupings and are seen as reprisal attacks for Irish republican violence.

These include the fatal shooting of an off duty policeman by the Irish National Liberation Army, an IRA splinter group which has never formally called a ceasefire. The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year.

The IRA has not struck in Northern Ireland itself for several weeks, prompting speculation that the guerrillas are observing an unofficial truce while Sinn Fein holds exploratory talks with officials serving Britain's new Labour government.
Sinn Fein is barred from Northern Ireland's peace talks grouping Irish nationalists and pro-British Unionists until its guerrilla backers end their war against British rule.
